title: Nonengagement and Unsuccessful Engagement with Feedback in Lower Secondary Education: The Role of Student Characteristics https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0361476X25000281
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), March 31, 2025 — original paper:
summary: This page covers Meyer, Jansen, and Fleckenstein's study of feedback uptake in a German writing-revision task with automated feedback, which distinguishes two distinct failure modes: nonengagement (making no revisions at all after feedback) and unsuccessful engagement (revising but not actually improving the work). The headline numbers are striking: 20 percent of lower secondary students did not engage with feedback at all, and a further 47.3 percent engaged unsuccessfully -- meaning that simply providing feedback failed to translate into improvement for roughly two-thirds of students. The authors trace both outcomes to individual student characteristics: male students, students with lower cognitive ability, students with lower English grades, and less conscientious students were all less likely to engage successfully. Barton draws out the practical implication that feedback is not self-executing -- teachers need to actively monitor whether and how students are using it, for instance via dashboards in digital systems, and should expect that a uniform feedback approach will underserve a substantial share of the class, particularly those with lower prior performance or weaker self-regulation.
points: In this study, 20% of students did not engage with feedback at all, and a further 47.3% engaged unsuccessfully -- revising without improving.
Nonengagement and unsuccessful engagement were both predicted by individual student characteristics: gender, cognitive ability, language proficiency, initial performance, and conscientiousness.
Male students and students with lower cognitive ability scores were less likely to engage successfully with feedback.
Teacher dashboards in digital learning systems can help identify students who are not engaging, or engaging unsuccessfully, enabling targeted intervention.
A one-size-fits-all approach to delivering feedback is unlikely to work, since students engage with it very differently depending on individual characteristics.
quotes: Findings show that 20% of students did not engage, 47% unsuccessfully engaged in a text revision. We focused on the role of individual differences in feedback engagement

The study found that 20% of lower secondary students did not make any revisions after receiving feedback (nonengagement), and 47.3% made revisions but did not improve their performance (unsuccessful engagement)
Gender: Male students were less likely to engage and successfully engage with feedback compared to female students
Cognitive Abilities: Students with lower cognitive ability scores were less likely to engage with feedback

Computer-based systems can assist teachers in identifying students who need support with feedback. Monitoring student feedback behavior through teacher dashboards can help detect students who are not engaging or are engaging unsuccessfully, allowing teachers to provide targeted interventions

There is a need to tailor feedback delivery to individual student characteristics. Recognizing that students engage with feedback differently based on their individual differences suggests that a one-size-fits-all approach to feedback may not be effective
